Lewis Pugh and his biggest swim yet

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
In 1875, Captain Matthew Webb became the first person to swim from Dover to Calais. Since then, some 1,800 people have swum across the English Channel. But no one has ever swum its entire length. Until this summer.

On the 12th July extreme swimmer, Lewis Pugh donned his goggles, swimming cap and speedo and got into the water at Land’s End, Cornwall UK and started his biggest challenge yet. He is aiming to swim the full length of the English Channel, from Land’s End to Dover. This 560 km distance is the equivalent to 16 English Channel crossings and will take an estimated 50 days depending on tide and weather.

In his words “ I am undertaking my toughest swim yet so that I can call …on all the governments of the world to strengthen our ocean protection.”

Lewis Pugh’s mission is to clean up our oceans “ our world needs clean and healthy seas. And we are the only ones who can make that happen.” This swim will mark the beginning of a worldwide campaign to ensure that 30% of our oceans are fully protected by 2030.

Since the start it’s been a riveting 13 days. Lewis is made for television: his pieces to camera; interviews; the visuals of the swim and the team work between the boat and his swim make great television- his encounters with the dolphins, sun fish and sharks and not so wonderful jelly fish, the visuals of the plastic pollution, the crew’s dancing on deck to keep Lewis motivated and the people from extreme swimmers to surfers to just people who like swimming who have joined Lewis on sections of his swim….

But it’s Lewis deeper insight into his mission that stays with you which is maybe why Prince Charles met up with him on Day 5 in St Agnes, Lewis wearing sneakers and shorts made for a much more intimate meeting than the usual Royal encounter.




Further information:
Lewis is in Day 13 of his swim and he has already encountered plastic pollution: “ we need to change the tide of plastic pollution by stopping the amount of plastic poring into our oceans…”

Carte Blanche has along history with Lewis Pugh, from his first Ice swim to his swim at the bottom of Mount Everest he has entertained and enlightened us, now on his greatest challenge yet an insert on him on the last days of his swim, using visuals from the entire swim.

Courage is just a muscle.

Script:


V/O 20 sec
On Wednesday extreme swimmer Lewis Pugh walked out of the water, up Dover’s Shakespeare Beach exhausted and exhilarated. He had swum the the English Channel.
Not the crossing but all 560 km’s of it …. the first person to swim its entire length.

John: That’s one hell of a journey
Lewis: It’s a once in a life time swim
John Just the once!

V/O 10 and a half sec
Lewis was born in Plymouth on this very coast, but grew up and lives in South Africa…
This epic journey began on the 12th July; Day 1 of The Long Swim.

Lewis: I am apprehensive because its such a mammoth long swim it’s been months and months of planning and preparation and finally I’m here it’s going to happen, see you in Dover

V/O 9 sec
At Lands End in Cornwall, Lewis entered the water, wearing only swimming cap, goggles and a Speedo.

V/O 9 and a half sec
44 days later, we caught up with Lewis in Eastbourne , about 70 swimming kilometres from Dover Beach, and boarded his boat the Aquila.

John : Lewis the end is in sight how are you feeling?
Lewis: I have never been more physically or emotionally exhausted it’s the equivalent 16 crossings of the English Channel back to back the sheer distance of this day after day week after week, physically I couldn’t imagine anything tougher.

V/O 19 sec
Every day – weather permitting- for the past 49 days Lewis has got up and dived into the water, his goal to swim 10kms a day …
Channel Swimming Association Rules are adhered to with every aspect of the swim recorded and logged.

Up Sound : 3 2 1 go

V/O 5 sec
Stephen the skipper drops Lewis at the exact co ordinates of the day before.

Lewis: The English Channel is one of the most tidal places in the world so the skipper looks at all the tide time tables and tries to work out exactly when the time is to swim so that timing crucial.
John: In retrospect was 10 kms a day realistic or could you have been a bit easier on your self?
Lewis: It was probably realistic that I could do 10 kms a day equivalent of swimming from Robben Island to Three Anchor Bay so it’s a significant distance. What I probably didn’t take account of was how many bad weather days we would have during expedition and then suddenly you have a wild day, swimming out in those wild conditions, my arm moving up and down and my body moving all over the place it is extremely taxing I just say to my self hopefully tomorrow things will improve and just keep hoping Lewis.

Up Sound: Lewis It was a washing machine out there and you are going round and round and I am just saying keep calm keep calm just keep calm

V/O 5 and a half sec
The point of the Long Swim is not the swim, but the message behind it

Up Sound: Lewis: It just drives me nuts this stuff people let off all these balloons showing love to friends and relatives or whatever it is and it just litters our beaches.

V/O 14 sec
……..The urgent need for marine conservation and the preservation of our oceans. It’s a call to governments, to leaders to fully protect at least 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030.

Lewis: I am absolutely single minded on the outcome which I am trying to achieve to get the UK government to understand the seriousness of the situation so around the 7 square km of UK waters are fully protected and the waters around the UK are 750 000 square km its astonishing so I try to constantly focus on that so when things do get tough that is something which I want to change.
John: The ambition is a third by 2030?
Lewis: What the scientists are saying is very clear, unless we set aside 30% of the worlds oceans by 2030 we are on a very dangerous trajectory.

V/O 14 sec
And even out of the water Lewis tirelessly delivered his message, he cleaned beaches, spoke to marine conservationists and government ministers. He even met Prince Charles wearing only shorts and flip flops.

Lewis: Its one of the big issues I face which is trying to get access to heads of state to environment leader trying to get them to make decisions today which will protect our oceans. Our oceans are telling us right now that its over.

Link
Lewis is an adventure swimmer who is prepared quiet literally in the ends of the earth to spread his message and despite his ability to swim in all manner of conditions and it was his ability to swim in freezing temp that really grabbed the headlines.

V/O 7 sec
In 2005 Lewis swam the icy waters of the Arctic to raise awareness about the dangers of climate change.

Lewis: I did a swim over there on the edge of the Arctic Sea Ice in 2005 and the water was 3 degree centigrade I went back last year the water was no longer 3 it was 10 degrees centigrade if you’ve got ice in 10 degree centigrade water that ice will melt.
John The knock on effect could be extraordinary?
Lewis: Correct, It’s runaway away climate change in that part of the Arctic.

Link
Lewis is back in the water and heading towards Dover 70 kms that way and that distance must seem every bit as challenging as the 400 kms he’ s already done.

V/O 10 sec
Keeping Lewis, motivated stroke after stroke was a team effort…guest swimmers jumped in with him for a short distance, …. His support crew spurred him on.

John: Two hours ahead of you Lewis feeling strong?
Lewis: Yes it’s another 60kms to Dover I’m not going to stop until get to Dover…it’s just a question of putting one stroke in front of the next.

V/O 11 sec
Meals and snacks were hugely important on the swim… every hour Lewis was burning 900 calories; every day 10 000 calories …

Link
When the weather wasn’t conspiring against him Lewis he was dealing with persistent pain in his shoulder but it seems the most persistent threat to this expedition has come from an unlikely source arch nemesis the jelly fish.

Lewis: What really surprised me on this swim was terms of wild life ..a few dolphin but on the whole very very little and lots of jelly fish and that’s a function of climate change with the warming waters around the UK jelly fish are moving in so much more jelly fish.
John: The jelly fish sent to torment you?
Lewis: There is no easy way to swim around jelly fish sometimes you have to swim through the jelly fish…painful especially when you are swimming at night and they all come up Up Sound WHISTLE AND OUT OUT its almost as if they were saying you will not get to the English Channel unless you get past us.

V/O 4 sec
And apart from the jelly fish plenty of plastics….

Lewis: It’s a Pandemic there is literally no part of our oceans which is free of plastic pollution I’m finding it high up Arctic down in Antarctica everywhere in between on the surface under the sea autopsies birds and fish inside when you eat fish now you are eating plastic we have to rid ourselves of single use plastic as quickly as possible straw cup cutlery gets into the ocean.

V/O 11 sec
As the suns sets on Day 44..Lewis continues his steady strokes, every stroke getting him closer to the White Cliffs of Dover..

John: So skipper about an hour into it seems to be going pretty smoothly?
Stephen Praetorius
Skipper:
We have got about a 15 knot tail wind so we are going to swim into the night tonight we are under pressure we have a long way to go yet and we are literally right on the swim rate.

Up Sound Clapping Thanks Boss

Lewis When skippers happy I am happy you know it’s a very close relationship the two of us have he has got to go out and find the currents and get me into the current and when he does not get me into the current I can see the disappointment on his face, and when he does get me into the current and when he does and I am swimming fast and hard then he’s happy and I am happy.
Up Sound If we get it right you are going to go racing through there and you saw how it was building this afternoon when you came out,
Lewis: There has been so much support from SA from Britain from all over the world. You know for me if you were to cut this swim down to what it actually is it is a fight for justice when we leave our children with an ocean that is unsustainable just cant do that its that simple.

V/O 7 sec
As Lewis swam into Dover Beach, his monumental swim finally over…..

APPLAUSE

V/O 8 sec
And after touching the harbour wall Lewis Pugh becomes the first person to swim the length of the English Channel,

Well done Lewis Cheers… Exhausted and exhilarated in equal measure.

V/O 6 and a half sec
but in Lewis’s words it’s not about breaking records but bringing the message home.


Promo 10 sec

Battling punishing weather conditions and icy waters, extreme swimmer Lewis Pugh’ s biggest challenge yet - swimming the entire length of the English Channel.

Promo 15 sec
From taking on his first ice swim to swimming below the summit of Mount Everest , Lewis Pugh has conquered his fears for decades. This week he finished his greatest challenge to date – swimming the entire length of the English Channel.
